## Proof

Let $\alpha = i - \sqrt{2}$. The extension $\mathbb{Q}(i, \sqrt{2})/\mathbb{Q}$ has Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$, generated by the automorphisms
$$\sigma: i \mapsto -i,\ \sqrt{2}\mapsto \sqrt{2}, \qquad \tau: i\mapsto i,\ \sqrt{2}\mapsto -\sqrt{2}.$$

Applying these to $\alpha$ gives the four conjugates:
$$\alpha = i-\sqrt{2},\quad \sigma(\alpha) = -i-\sqrt{2},\quad \tau(\alpha) = i+\sqrt{2},\quad \sigma\tau(\alpha) = -i+\sqrt{2}.$$

The given hypothesis $\mathbb{Q}(i,\sqrt{2}) = \mathbb{Q}(i+\sqrt{2})$ confirms that $[\mathbb{Q}(i,\sqrt{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$, so the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ has degree $4$ and equals the product over all four conjugates:
$$m(x) = (x-(i-\sqrt{2}))(x-(-i-\sqrt{2}))(x-(i+\sqrt{2}))(x-(-i+\sqrt{2})).$$

Pair the factors so that each pair eliminates $i$:
$$(x-(i-\sqrt{2}))(x-(-i-\sqrt{2})) = (x+\sqrt{2}-i)(x+\sqrt{2}+i) = (x+\sqrt{2})^2+1 = x^2+2\sqrt{2}\,x+3,$$
$$(x-(i+\sqrt{2}))(x-(-i+\sqrt{2})) = (x-\sqrt{2}-i)(x-\sqrt{2}+i) = (x-\sqrt{2})^2+1 = x^2-2\sqrt{2}\,x+3.$$

Now multiply, eliminating $\sqrt{2}$:
$$m(x) = (x^2+2\sqrt{2}\,x+3)(x^2-2\sqrt{2}\,x+3) = (x^2+3)^2 - (2\sqrt{2}\,x)^2 = x^4+6x^2+9-8x^2.$$

Thus
$$\boxed{m(x) = x^4 - 2x^2 + 9}.$$

**Verification.** With $\alpha = i-\sqrt{2}$:
$$\alpha^2 = (i-\sqrt{2})^2 = -1-2i\sqrt{2}+2 = 1-2i\sqrt{2},$$
$$\alpha^4 = (1-2i\sqrt{2})^2 = 1-4i\sqrt{2}-8 = -7-4i\sqrt{2}.$$
Therefore
$$\alpha^4 - 2\alpha^2 + 9 = (-7-4i\sqrt{2}) - 2(1-2i\sqrt{2}) + 9 = -7-4i\sqrt{2}-2+4i\sqrt{2}+9 = 0.$$

The polynomial $x^4 - 2x^2 + 9$ has rational coefficients and vanishes at $i-\sqrt{2}$, as required.
